title: Advanced Data Transformation with JSONata, JMESPath, and Expressions
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Advanced Data Transformation with JSONata, JMESPath, and Expressions ##### Twenty-three mapping steps, one expression An integration between a booking platform and an accounting system had grown to 23 sequential steps in Make.com. Nineteen of them were transformations: uppercase a country code, format a date, sum an array, concatenate a name, default a missing field, extract the first non-cancelled line item. Each step cost an operation. Each was independently configured, independently breakable, and collectively impossible to read. When the source added a nested `tax_breakdown` array, the change required editing seven of them. Rewritten as a single JSONata expression, the same transformation became one module and about thirty lines of declarative code — version-controllable, testable in isolation, and readable top to bottom. That is the shift this article is about: from **imperative step-by-step mapping** to **declarative transformation**, where you describe the target shape and let the engine work out the traversal. ##### Why declarative beats step chains Four concrete advantages, and they compound: **Atomicity.** One expression either produces the whole output or fails visibly. Nineteen steps can half-succeed, leaving a partially transformed record downstream. **Readability.** The output shape is literally visible in the expression's structure. A chain of steps requires opening each one to reconstruct what it builds. **Testability.** An expression is a pure function of its input. You can run it against fixtures — including the awkward ones — outside the platform entirely, and diff the results. **Cost and performance.** On operation-billed platforms, collapsing nineteen modules into one is a direct 95% reduction on that segment. In code, one traversal beats nineteen. The trade-off is real and worth naming: expressions are denser, and a colleague who is comfortable clicking through visual steps may find a 30-line JSONata expression opaque. Mitigate with comments, formatting, and a test fixture that documents intent. For genuinely complex logic — multi-way branching with side effects — a Code node is often clearer than a heroic one-liner. ##### The three languages **jq** is the command-line standard for JSON. Pipeline-oriented, extremely expressive, available everywhere, and the right tool for shell scripts, CI pipelines and ad-hoc exploration. **JMESPath** is a specification-driven query language, embedded in the AWS CLI (`--query`), Ansible and many SDKs. More constrained than jq — deliberately — with a formal grammar and predictable semantics. **JSONata** is the most powerful for *transformation* specifically, because it can construct arbitrary output objects. It is the expression language inside n8n, IBM App Connect and several iPaaS products, and its `$` function library covers strings, numbers, dates, arrays and higher-order functions. Roughly: **jq for the terminal, JMESPath for querying inside AWS tooling, JSONata for building output structures in integration platforms.** ##### A worked payload Everything below transforms this: ```json { "booking": { "id": "BK-4471", "created": "2026-03-14T09:12:44Z", "customer": { "first": " ananya ", "last": "RAO", "email": "Ananya@Example.COM", "country": "in" }, "items": [ { "sku": "ROOM-DLX", "nights": 3, "rate": 4500.00, "status": "confirmed" }, { "sku": "BRKFST", "nights": 3, "rate": 450.00, "status": "confirmed" }, { "sku": "SPA-60", "nights": 1, "rate": 2500.00, "status": "cancelled" } ], "notes": null } } ``` ##### Mapping: reshaping each element **JSONata** — the `.` operator maps over arrays automatically, and `{...}` constructs objects: ```javascript booking.items.{ "code": sku, "quantity": nights, "unitPrice": rate, "lineTotal": nights * rate } ``` **jq** — explicit iteration with `map`: ```bash jq '.booking.items | map({ code: .sku, quantity: .nights, unitPrice: .rate, lineTotal: (.nights * .rate) })' booking.json ``` **JMESPath** — projections with a multiselect hash: ```text booking.items[*].{code: sku, quantity: nights, unitPrice: rate} ``` Note JMESPath's limitation immediately: it has no arithmetic, so `lineTotal` is impossible. That constraint is why it is a *query* language rather than a transformation language. ##### Filtering: selecting a subset **JSONata** uses `[...]` predicates directly on the path: ```javascript booking.items[status = "confirmed" and rate > 1000] ``` **jq** uses `select` inside a map, or the shorthand: ```bash jq '[.booking.items[] | select(.status == "confirmed" and .rate > 1000)]' booking.json ``` **JMESPath** uses filter projections: ```text booking.items[?status == 'confirmed' && rate > `1000`] ``` The backticks in JMESPath denote a JSON literal — a genuine gotcha, since `rate > 1000` without them is parsed as a field reference and silently matches nothing. ##### Aggregating: collapsing to a value **JSONata** has aggregate functions and `$sum` over a mapped array: ```javascript $sum(booking.items[status = "confirmed"].(nights * rate)) ``` That reads left to right: filter to confirmed, compute `nights * rate` for each, sum. The `.(expression)` syntax applies an expression per item — this is the construct that makes JSONata genuinely powerful. **jq**: ```bash jq '[.booking.items[] | select(.status=="confirmed") | .nights * .rate] | add' booking.json ``` **JMESPath** can `sum()` a projection but cannot multiply, so aggregation of derived values is out of reach: ```text sum(booking.items[?status == 'confirmed'].rate) ``` ##### Conditionals, functions, and string handling Real mapping needs defaults, case normalization and date formatting. JSONata handles all of it inline: ```javascript { "reference": booking.id, "issuedOn": $substringBefore(booking.created, "T"), "customer": { /* trim, title-case, and join the name parts */ "name": $trim($uppercase($substring(booking.customer.first, 0, 1)) & $lowercase($substring($trim(booking.customer.first), 1))) & " " & $uppercase($substring($trim(booking.customer.last), 0, 1)) & $lowercase($substring($trim(booking.customer.last), 1)), "email": $lowercase($trim(booking.customer.email)), "country": $uppercase(booking.customer.country) }, "lines": booking.items[status = "confirmed"].{ "code": sku, "qty": nights, "rate": rate, "total": nights * rate }, "subtotal": $sum(booking.items[status = "confirmed"].(nights * rate)), "tax": $round($sum(booking.items[status = "confirmed"].(nights * rate)) * 0.18, 2), "total": $round($sum(booking.items[status = "confirmed"].(nights * rate)) * 1.18, 2), /* explicit default for a nullable field */ "notes": booking.notes ? booking.notes : "", /* derived flag: did anything get cancelled? */ "hasCancellations": $count(booking.items[status = "cancelled"]) > 0 } ``` The functions worth committing to memory: `$string`, `$number`, `$trim`, `$uppercase`, `$lowercase`, `$substring`, `$split`, `$join`, `$replace`, `$match`, `$contains`, `$sum`, `$count`, `$average`, `$max`, `$min`, `$round`, `$floor`, `$abs`, `$now`, `$fromMillis`, `$toMillis`, `$map`, `$filter`, `$reduce`, `$sort`, `$distinct`, `$merge`, `$keys`, `$exists`, and `$type`. Two JSONata behaviours that trip people up. **Singleton collapse**: a filter matching exactly one item returns the object, not a one-element array — wrap in `[...]` when you need array shape guaranteed. And **absent is not null**: `$exists(field)` distinguishes a missing key from an explicit `null`, which matters constantly. ##### Schema mapping between systems The production application is a **canonical mapping layer**: each source system maps into your internal schema, and your internal schema maps out to each destination. Two systems require two mappings rather than one; ten systems require twenty rather than forty-five. ```mermaid flowchart LR S1[Booking platform
nested, camelCase] -->|map in| C[(Canonical
schema)] S2[Legacy CSV feed
flat, snake_case] -->|map in| C S3[Partner API
arrays of pairs] -->|map in| C C -->|map out| D1[Accounting system] C -->|map out| D2[Warehouse] C -->|map out| D3[Analytics] ``` Store each mapping as a **named, versioned expression file** in Git, with fixtures: ```text mappings/ ├── in/booking-platform.v2.jsonata ├── in/legacy-csv.v1.jsonata ├── out/accounting.v3.jsonata └── fixtures/ ├── booking-platform/01-happy.json + 01-happy.expected.json ├── booking-platform/02-all-cancelled.json ├── booking-platform/03-missing-country.json └── booking-platform/04-empty-items.json ``` A test harness then runs every fixture through its mapping and diffs against the expected output: ```python import json, pathlib, jsonata # pip install jsonata-python def test_mapping(expr_path: pathlib.Path, fixture_dir: pathlib.Path) -> None: expr = jsonata.Jsonata(expr_path.read_text()) for src in sorted(fixture_dir.glob("*.json")): if src.name.endswith(".expected.json"): continue expected_path = src.with_suffix(".expected.json") actual = expr.evaluate(json.loads(src.read_text())) expected = json.loads(expected_path.read_text()) assert actual == expected, f"{src.name}\n got: {actual}\nwant: {expected}" print(f" ok {src.name}") ``` This turns transformation into ordinary, reviewable, regression-tested software — which is the real point of the declarative approach. ##### Common pitfalls - **Singleton collapse** in JSONata producing an object where downstream code expects an array. - **Confusing missing with null** — use `$exists()` rather than truthiness. - **JMESPath literals without backticks**, silently matching nothing. - **jq quoting in shells** — use single quotes around the filter and `--arg` for variables. - **Assuming array order is stable** across API responses; sort explicitly when it matters. - **Building unreadable one-liners.** Format across lines, add `/* comments */` (JSONata supports them), and split genuinely complex logic. - **No fixtures.** An untested expression is a silent-corruption risk, because it usually produces *something*. - **Arithmetic on strings** — `"3" * 4` behaves differently across engines; coerce with `$number()` first. - **Losing precision on money** — round explicitly at the end, and prefer integer minor units where you can. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: take a complex nested payload and, in **JSONata (inside n8n)** and separately in **jq**, write single expressions that flatten it, filter an inner array by a condition, and produce an aggregated summary field. Use the booking payload above or one of your own. Doing it twice in two languages is the point — the differences illuminate what each is actually for, and jqplay.org and try.jsonata.org both give you instant feedback loops. The mini project is the **reusable schema-mapping layer**: convert records between two very different system schemas — renamed keys, nested↔flat, arrays, defaults for missing fields — using JSONata or jq expressions, **with test cases proving correctness**. Build the fixture set first, including all-cancelled, empty-array and missing-field cases, then write the expression until every fixture passes. That order is deliberate and it is how transformation bugs get caught before production. For the assignment, write and explain **three expressions — one map, one filter, one aggregate** — on a sample dataset, and argue why **declarative transformation beats many manual mapping steps**. Anchor the argument in the four concrete advantages: atomicity, readability, testability, and cost. If you have a real before/after operation count from your own workflow, lead with it. ##### Key takeaways - Declarative expressions replace long chains of mapping steps with one atomic, readable, testable transformation — and on operation-billed platforms, a large cost reduction. - jq is the terminal standard, JMESPath the constrained query language embedded in AWS tooling, JSONata the most capable for constructing output objects in iPaaS platforms. - Master the three core operations — map (`.{ }` / `map()`), filter (`[predicate]` / `select()`), aggregate (`$sum` / `add`) — plus conditionals, defaults and string functions. - Build a canonical schema with map-in and map-out expressions per system; this turns quadratic integration growth into linear. - Store expressions as versioned files with fixtures and an automated diff test — including empty, missing and all-filtered-out cases.
